findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the wrong behavior
findings.body: The test docstring says "Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages", but the final assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` checks that NO offset is committed. The implementation in OrderedQueueWorker.run always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in the `finally` block, even when the result_processor raises an exception. So after both messages are processed (one with an error, one successfully), the offset WILL be committed at 102 (next to read after 101). The test contradicts the implementation: it should assert that the offset IS committed (e.g., `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`), demonstrating that errors don't block offset commits. Additionally, the test sleeps only 0.2 seconds after the loop break, but the commit thread runs every 1 second, making the test flaky depending on timing.

findings.title: --mode help text does not mention thread-queue-parallel
findings.body: The `uptime_options()` `--mode` help text reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." After this PR, the choice list adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` but the help text was not updated. Users running `sentry run uptime-results --help` will see the new mode accepted but get no explanation of what it does or when to prefer it over the other modes.

findings.title: assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue) is stripped under python -O
findings.body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the line `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is used as a runtime type guard before accessing `message.value.partition`/`offset`. Python strips `assert` statements when run with `-O` (which some production deployments use for performance). Without the assert, the code would raise `AttributeError` on non-BrokerValue messages, which is then swallowed by the generic `except Exception` that tries to recover by adding/completing the offset — but `message.value.partition`/`offset` will still AttributeError. The check should be an explicit `if not isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue): return/log/handle` rather than an assert.

findings.title: Offsets are marked complete even when result_processor raises
findings.body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` even when the result_processor raised an exception. This silently drops processing failures: the offset is committed as if the message succeeded, and the message will not be retried. For an uptime consumer this means a failing check-in (e.g., transient DB error) is permanently lost. Either the offset should only be marked complete on success, or failures should be routed to the DLQ/stale topic, or the comment in the code should clearly call out that this is intentional at-least-once-with-loss-on-error semantics. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` actually codifies the wrong expectation (see separate finding).

findings.title: hash()-based group routing is not stable across restarts
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python randomizes the string hash seed between processes by default (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same group_key will map to a different queue index after a restart. The class docstring claims "Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue" and "No dynamic reassignment that could break ordering" — this is only true within a single process lifetime. Across restarts, in-flight unprocessed items from a group will not be drained in order relative to new arrivals. The docstring should clarify the lifetime guarantee, or a stable hash (e.g. hashlib) should be used.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions does not verify concurrency
findings.body: The test creates two subscriptions, sends one message to each, and asserts `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2`. Nothing in the test actually verifies that the two messages were processed concurrently (e.g., by instrumenting the result_processor to hold a lock and observing that the two calls overlap in time, or by checking that they were dispatched to different workers/queues). The test name advertises a concurrency property it does not exercise.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit uses private arroyo internals
findings.body: The Kafka integration test drives the consumer via `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` — these are private arroyo methods whose behavior is not part of the public contract. It also creates the `UptimeResultsStrategyFactory` before the `override_settings(KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES=...)` context, and the factory's `create_with_partitions` is monkey-patched in place, so the test is not actually exercising the real consumer wiring under `override_settings`. Combined with the `mock_processor` doing nothing, the test mostly verifies that the offset-tracker/commit-loop machinery, when hand-driven, produces offset 5 — it does not validate that the production code path commits correctly. Consider using the public `processor.run()` or running the consumer in a thread with a real termination signal.

findings.title: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate has no test coverage
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` (line 340-342) is not exercised by any test in `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py` or the uptime test file. `terminate()` differs from `close()` in that it does not join the commit thread. Since arroyo's StreamProcessor may invoke `terminate()` on shutdown, a regression that double-shuts-down the queue pool or hangs the commit thread would go undetected. A simple test that calls `strategy.terminate()` after some work has been submitted would cover this path.

findings.title: Sentry transaction name in OrderedQueueWorker is hardcoded to monitors.*
findings.body: The transaction name in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This module lives under `sentry.remote_subscriptions.consumers.queue_consumer` and is now used by the uptime consumer (`identifier="uptime"`) and potentially other consumers. Hardcoding the `monitors.` prefix will produce misleading transaction names like `monitors.uptime.worker_3` in Sentry's performance UI, making it harder to filter and group transactions correctly. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or removed.
